channel.title: The Pointe at Kirby Gate: Senior Living News
channel.description: Senior housing, senior care and caregiving news from trusted publishers, gathered every day by our team. The summaries are ours; the full stories belong to their publishers.

item.title: Hearing loss linked to more falls and fear of falling in adults 65 and older, national study finds
item.description: A study in the Journal of the American Geriatrics Society drew on national survey data from 4,745 Medicare beneficiaries age 65 and older, collected between 2011 and 2022. Both hearing loss measured by testing and hearing trouble people noticed in daily life were associated with falls and with fear of falling. Among those with everyday hearing difficulty, about 40% reported a fall in the prior year, and a similar share said they were afraid of falling. Hearing aid use was not tied to lower odds of either outcome. Because the study shows an association, it cannot prove that hearing loss causes falls. Why it matters: Changes in a parent's hearing may be worth raising with their doctor as part of a broader talk about fall risk.

item.title: About 4.3 million Medicare enrollees must pick a new plan by Dec. 7 after insurers leave some markets
item.description: NPR reports that an estimated 4.3 million people will need to choose a new Medicare Advantage or prescription drug plan for 2027 because insurers are pulling out of certain markets. Open enrollment ends December 7, and coverage chosen now begins January 1. People whose Advantage plan is ending and who take no action are moved to traditional Medicare, which does not include drug coverage by itself, so they would need a separate Part D plan to keep most prescriptions covered. The story also walks through other 2027 changes and encourages enrollees to read their plan notices and compare options before the deadline. Why it matters: If a parent got a notice that their plan is ending, there are only days left to compare options; a benefits counselor can help.

item.title: AARP report: family caregivers have about 40% more poor mental health days than other adults
item.description: A new report from AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving, part of the Caregiving in the US research series, looks at the health of people who care for relatives and friends. Family caregivers report roughly 40% more days of poor mental health than the average U.S. adult. Money pressure makes a large difference: among caregivers under high financial strain, about three in four report high emotional stress, compared with about three in ten other caregivers, and they are about twice as likely to rate their own health as fair or poor. The findings put a spotlight on caregivers' own well-being as part of planning a loved one's care. Why it matters: A family caregiver's own health and stress belong in the decision about when to bring in more support.

item.title: Shelby County deputies help MIFA deliver meals to homebound seniors
item.description: Staff from the Shelby County Sheriff's Office joined the Metropolitan Inter-Faith Association (MIFA) last week to help bring meals to older adults in Memphis. WREG reports that more than 30 sheriff's office employees delivered boxes of shelf-stable food, with five meals in each box. MIFA's Meals on Wheels program serves homebound seniors age 60 and older with daily meal deliveries, and seniors are referred to the program through the Aging Commission of the Mid-South. Why it matters: If you worry about a parent eating well at home, the Aging Commission of the Mid-South can tell you how meal delivery referrals work.

item.title: New guide: selling a parent's home to pay for assisted living
item.description: Our new guide is for families weighing whether to sell a parent's house when they move to assisted living or memory care. It starts with the family conversation: involving your parent, confirming who has legal authority to sign, and keeping siblings informed. It then explains in plain language how the IRS home sale exclusion works, including a special rule for people who can no longer care for themselves, with links to the official IRS publications. It is general information, and families are encouraged to confirm details with a tax professional or attorney. Why it matters: A clear starting point for the questions families ask most before listing a parent's home.

item.title: AARP: how to talk with relatives about a parent's changes at the holiday table
item.description: Holiday gatherings are often when siblings and other relatives first see how much an older parent has changed. AARP's caregiving guide suggests keeping these conversations calm and specific: skip blaming statements, ask relatives what they have noticed about the parent's walking, speech or memory, and turn offers of help into concrete tasks someone can take on. It also encourages caregivers to let others share the load rather than carrying it alone through the season. Why it matters: Thanksgiving is a natural time for families to notice a parent needs more support and to start planning together, before a crisis forces the decision.

item.title: Florida drafts its first rules for a separate memory care license in assisted living
item.description: Florida's health care agency has started writing rules for a new memory care specialty license for assisted living communities, created by a 2026 state law. The draft would set minimum direct-care staffing levels for memory care residents, require licensed nurses to give their medications, and require a community that advertises memory care to hold the license. Provider groups told McKnight's Senior Living they have concerns about parts of the draft, and the state held a public workshop in mid-November. The rules are not final and could change. Why it matters: States are starting to set their own standards for memory care, so families comparing communities can ask how staffing, training and medication care are handled.

item.title: J.D. Power: family satisfaction with assisted living and memory care slipped in 2026, while independent living rose
item.description: J.D. Power's 2026 U.S. Senior Living Satisfaction Study found that family members and other decision-makers for assisted living and memory care residents were somewhat less satisfied than a year earlier. The segment's overall score fell four points to 863 on a 1,000-point scale. Four of the six areas measured declined: community staff, resident activities, the apartment or living unit, and buildings and grounds. Independent living moved the other way, with resident satisfaction up 14 points to 767. The assisted living and memory care results come from 860 responses collected from June through August 2026. Why it matters: The study tracks how families rate the parts of assisted living and memory care they see most, including staff, daily activities and living spaces.

item.title: IRS raises 2027 limits on long-term care insurance premiums that can count as a medical expense
item.description: The IRS published its tax year 2027 inflation adjustments on Nov. 5 in Revenue Procedure 2026-35. They include the age-based caps on how much of a premium for a tax-qualified long-term care insurance policy can count as a medical expense. As summarized by the American Association for Long-Term Care Insurance, the cap for people over 70 rises to $6,290 from $6,200 in 2026, and the cap for ages 61 to 70 rises to $5,030 from $4,960. The IRS also raised the daily limit on certain tax-free long-term care benefits to $445 from $430. The premiums count only within the usual rules for itemized medical-expense deductions. For questions about a specific situation, talk to a benefits counselor or an elder law attorney. Why it matters: Families of someone over 70 who holds a tax-qualified long-term care policy may see a slightly higher limit on deductible premiums for tax year 2027.

item.title: First ACSI senior care study finds families rate communities higher than residents do
item.description: The American Customer Satisfaction Index released its first Senior Care Communities Study, based on 2,830 completed surveys. Family members scored their satisfaction at 73 on a 100-point scale, and residents scored theirs at 62. Families scored higher across the study's customer experience measures, and the gap was widest on trust, at 75 for families and 59 for residents. Assisted living had the highest satisfaction of the settings studied. The largest differences between residents and families were in skilled nursing and independent living. More than a third of residents and family members said they had filed a complaint. Why it matters: A resident's own view of daily life can differ a lot from the family's, which matters when comparing communities or checking in after a move.

item.title: Report: staffing now takes about 48% of senior living revenue as residents need more care
item.description: Senior Housing News covers a new industry report that looks at why demand for senior living is strong while construction of new communities is not. One finding concerns staffing: it took an average of 48% of revenue in 2025, compared with 39% ten years earlier. The authors say the main driver is probably that residents now arrive needing more care than in the past, more than the extra staff required as buildings fill up. Why it matters: Few new communities and higher care needs can mean fewer openings, which is a reason for families to start looking early.

item.title: Medicare Part B premium will be $209.40 a month in 2027, up $6.50
item.description: The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has set the standard Medicare Part B premium for 2027 at $209.40 a month, an increase of $6.50 from $202.90 this year. The yearly Part B deductible will rise by $9, from $283 to $292. The agency says the increases mainly reflect projected growth in health care spending. People with higher incomes pay more than the standard amount. According to the Social Security Administration, enrollees can see their own 2027 premium in the message center of their my Social Security account starting in late November. Why it matters: Part B is usually taken out of the Social Security payment, so the new premium changes the monthly income a family has to plan with.

item.title: AARP: 11 ways family caregivers can ease holiday stress
item.description: AARP's guide for family caregivers suggests ways to make the holiday season more manageable. Its ideas include bringing in extra help, such as respite care or a hired helper for chores and decorating, and sharing the cooking by making meals potluck-style. It also suggests starting new traditions that fit what a loved one can comfortably do now, and keeping gatherings shorter with time set aside for rest. Why it matters: With Thanksgiving next week, small changes to the plan can make the day easier for the caregiver and for the person receiving care.

item.title: Researcher says dementia diagnosis is not keeping pace with new treatments as care needs grow
item.description: An Alzheimer's researcher at the University of Kansas told Senior Housing News that the system for diagnosing dementia has fallen behind the newer treatments now available. He pointed to memory clinic waitlists that can run for months and a shortage of dementia specialists as the main barriers. The article notes that 44% of assisted living residents live with Alzheimer's or another form of dementia, which makes earlier and faster diagnosis a growing concern for families and the communities that care for them. Why it matters: An earlier diagnosis gives a family more time to plan care and choose the right setting before a crisis.

item.title: Blood-test markers help estimate who may develop memory problems within 5 to 10 years, study finds
item.description: A study in JAMA Neurology looked at older adults who had no memory or thinking problems but whose tests showed Alzheimer's-related changes in the brain. Using long-running research groups, including the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging, researchers estimated each person's chance of developing mild cognitive impairment or dementia over 5 and 10 years. Higher starting levels of a blood marker called p-tau217 were tied to a greater risk, and risk also rose with age. The goal is clearer, personal risk estimates instead of a simple yes-or-no result. Families with questions about memory testing should talk to their doctor. Why it matters: Blood tests are entering memory checkups, so families may hear about these markers at a parent's next visit.

item.title: Social Security is notifying some Medicare enrollees who must confirm eligibility under new immigration-status rules
item.description: The Social Security Administration says a federal law enacted in July 2025 narrows who can be entitled to Medicare. Eligibility is now limited to U.S. citizens and nationals, lawful permanent residents and a few other specific immigration categories. SSA is mailing letters this month to current enrollees whose eligibility it cannot confirm or who no longer qualify, and it says Medicare coverage may end on February 1, 2027 for people whose eligibility is not confirmed. The agency notes the change does not affect eligibility for Social Security benefits or how they are paid. CMS actuaries estimate about 32,000 people will lose coverage. Why it matters: Families who help an older relative with mail should watch for these letters, since SSA says unconfirmed eligibility can end Medicare coverage on February 1.

item.title: New guide: choosing assisted living near East Memphis and Germantown
item.description: Our new guide is for families comparing assisted living close to home in East Memphis, Germantown and Collierville. It suggests starting with the relative who will visit most, driving the route at a real visiting hour, and keeping a parent's doctors, pharmacy and weekly routines within reach. It explains how Tennessee licenses assisted care living facilities, how to ask a community for its latest state survey, and how the Long-Term Care Ombudsman can help. It also covers what to look for when a parent has memory loss and ends with a checklist for comparing nearby communities. Why it matters: Distance narrows the list, but level of care, inspection history and a parent's routines decide the right fit.

item.title: Study links high-dose flu shots to lower Alzheimer's risk in adults 65 and older
item.description: Researchers at UTHealth Houston, publishing in the journal Neurology, compared older adults who received a high-dose flu vaccine with those who received the standard dose. In this large records-based study, the high-dose group was less likely to be diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease in the years that followed, and the link appeared stronger in women. Because the study was observational, it shows an association, not proof that the vaccine prevents Alzheimer's, and the authors call for further research. Why it matters: Flu season is here; families with an older parent can ask their doctor which flu vaccine is right for them.

item.title: New Congress expected to look harder at senior living ownership, staffing and affordability
item.description: Senior Housing News reports that the incoming Congress is likely to give senior living more attention. Lawmakers have signaled interest in how communities are owned and financed, including private equity and real estate investment structures, and in staffing and workforce practices. At the same time, industry groups see openings to work on affordability for middle-income older adults. Assisted living is regulated mainly by the states, and the industry's trade group says it plans to explain to lawmakers how assisted living differs from nursing homes. Why it matters: Families comparing communities can expect more public attention on who owns a community and how it is staffed, both good questions to ask on any tour.

item.title: CDC: nearly half of assisted living communities care for residents with dementia, heart disease, diabetes and depression
item.description: A new data brief from the CDC's National Center for Health Statistics, drawn from its 2025 national survey of residential care communities (the federal category that includes assisted living), found that 48% of communities had current residents living with each of four common chronic conditions: Alzheimer's disease or another dementia, heart disease, diabetes and depression. About 19% more reported three of the four. Communities with 11 or more beds, those outside metro areas and those in the Northeast and Midwest were more likely to report all four. Communities that did were also more likely to report resident emergency department visits, overnight hospital stays and falls. Why it matters: Many assisted living residents live with several chronic conditions at once, so it helps to ask any community how it supports dementia, diabetes, heart and mood-related care needs.
